an0655.user: Quick one — why is my CTR low on Performance Max? Actually the bigger thing bugging me: Meta-side I'm seeing 4.3 ROAS on ₹4L spend last 30 days, but Shopify last-click says 2.0 for the same period. Which number is the real one for my eyewear store?
an0655.assistant:
Forget CTR for a second — that's not your problem. Your problem is you're refereeing a fight between two dashboards that will never shake hands. Performance Max reports 4.3 because it uses modelled conversions and a 7-day-click window, so it claims credit for sales that would've happened anyway. Shopify last-click shows 2.0 because it only counts the final click and ignores every ad that warmed the buyer up. Both are biased in opposite directions. Post-iOS, this gap is structural, not a bug — the truth sits somewhere between 2.0 and 4.3, and no amount of staring will reconcile them.

So stop trying to pick a winner. Anchor on one number neither platform can spin: blended CAC = total ad spend ÷ actual new customers from Shopify. That's ₹4L divided by however many genuinely-new buyers you got — tag returning customers out. Manage to that figure month over month. If blended CAC sits comfortably under your contribution per new customer, you're fine regardless of what either ROAS claims.

Caveat: blended CAC blurs new vs repeat unless you separate them cleanly in Shopify, so get that tagging right before you trust the trend.

an0656.user: Running YouTube ads for my gym, here are the numbers, tell me what's wrong: last 8 weeks I pushed spend from ₹5L to ₹9.5L. AOV ₹2500, margin 49%. CAC was ₹595 at the start, now it's ₹869. ROAS dropped from 4.2 to 2.9. Why is it falling apart as I scale?
an0656.assistant:
Nothing's broken — you hit a ceiling and walked straight into it. You nearly doubled spend (₹5L → ₹9.5L) and ROAS slid 4.2 → 2.9 while CAC climbed ₹595 → ₹869. That's not a creative failure or a tracking glitch; that's saturation. Your efficient audience — people in your catchment who actually want a gym — is a finite pool. The first ₹5L bought the warmest, highest-intent reach. The extra ₹4.5L is buying colder, pricier impressions because the cheap intent is already exhausted. The CAC rising in near-lockstep with spend is the proof.

Check your contribution still holds: ₹2500 × 49% − ₹869 = ₹1225 − ₹869 = +₹356 per member. You're still profitable, so don't panic-cut. But more budget into the same channel just keeps dragging that ₹356 toward zero.

The lever isn't budget, it's new demand. Open a new pool before you spend another rupee here — fresh creative angles, a different audience (corporate tie-ups, ex-members win-back), or a second channel like local Meta/WhatsApp. Manufacture intent rather than mining the last drops of what's left.

Caveat: a gym is geographically capped, so your ceiling may genuinely be low — at some point the honest answer is 'this channel is maxed,' not 'try harder.'

an0657.user: Pasting my email numbers — CAC jumped 19% this week vs last week. Conversions this week were 115. I think the whole strategy is broken, I'm about to tear it down and rebuild from scratch. What's wrong?
an0657.assistant:
Don't tear anything down. A 19% CAC swing on 115 conversions is noise, not a trend — that base is small enough that a handful of orders landing a day later or a couple of pricier clicks moves the number that much. One week tells you almost nothing.

Reacting to a single noisy week is exactly how founders whipsaw their accounts into the ground: you change five things, next week reverts on its own, and now you can't tell what did what.

Do nothing this week. A real signal is the same direction holding for 3–4 weeks straight, or a swing big enough that it clearly can't be random — a 50%+ jump, not 19%. Until then, leave it running and keep logging the weekly number. Patience is the move here.

The real signal you're underweighting is the 29% 90-day repeat — for edtech that's a meaningful re-purchase/upsell base, which means LTV runs well past that first +₹380.

Lever: stop optimising CTR and stop reading ROAS as a verdict. Manage to contribution, and given those unit economics this account should be scaling spend, not defending a click-through rate.
